en: Śāriputra, regarding those who dispute the essential points of the various sūtras— one who holds such views, I do not permit to go forth or receive the precepts.
Śāriputra, regarding one who holds such views, I do not permit them to receive even a single sip of water for their own sustenance.
They make offerings,
yet they diligently cultivate the signless samādhi,
even grasping at signs within that signless samādhi.
This person penetrates the fact that the characteristics of all phenomena are but a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*).
The *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra*, in the "Recollection of the Buddha" chapter, says: "Evil spiritual friends..."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If there is a bhikṣu who instructs another bhikṣu, saying:

'You should mindfully recollect the Buddha, mindfully recollect the Dharma, mindfully recollect the Saṅgha, mindfully recollect the precepts, mindfully recollect generosity, and mindfully recollect the devas.'"
To teach that one should only love nirvāṇa as ultimately pure—
such a teaching is called a false teaching; that is,
to claim that what is a true teaching is a false teaching.
Śāriputra, one who teaches in such a manner is called a bad friend (pāpamitra).
Such a person is said to slander me and to assist the followers of external paths (tīrthika).
Furthermore, Śāriputra, such evil persons as these—
I do not permit them even to receive a single drink of water for their own sustenance.
Śāriputra, this mindfulness of the Buddha cuts off the path of speech and transcends all thoughts;
that which cannot be grasped as a thought is called mindfulness of the Buddha.
Śāriputra, all thoughts are characterized by quiescence;
one should accord with this Dharma.
This is precisely what is called the cultivation of mindfulness of the Buddha.
One should not mindfully contemplate the Buddha by means of form. Why is this?
To be mindful of form by grasping its marks and relishing its flavor constitutes consciousness.
That which is formless, colorless, objectless, and devoid of intrinsic nature—
this is called mindfulness of the Buddha.
Therefore, one should know that to be without discrimination, without grasping,
and without rejection is the true recollection of the Buddha.
The *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on Mindfulness of the Dharma," states:
"O Śāriputra, at that time, this person has nothing whatsoever; they are quiescent and without intrinsic nature."
Not accumulating various marks and extinguishing all dharmas—
this is called the cultivation of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Mindfulness of the Buddha means breaking through all wholesome and unwholesome discursive thoughts (*vitarka-vicāra*).
To be without applied thought and sustained thought, tranquil and without conceptualization—
this is called mindfulness of the Buddha. Why is this so?
One should not recollect the Buddhas through applied thought and sustained thought.
To be without applied thought and without sustained thought is called pure mindfulness of the Buddha, Śāriputra.
Śāriputra, all conceptualizations that arise according to one's thoughts are false views. They are, however,
in accordance with non-existence, without applied thought or sustained thought, and without arising or ceasing.
To penetrate this is called mindfulness of the Buddha.
Within such mindfulness, there is no greed and no attachment;
there is neither opposition nor compliance.
Without name and without form,
without thought and without speech—
this is what is called mindfulness of the Buddha.
Within this, there is not even the slightest subtle thought,
let alone coarse actions of body, speech, and mind.
It is a state where there is no action of body, speech, or mind.
Without thought and without discrimination,
empty, quiescent, and devoid of intrinsic nature, extinguishing all discursive investigation and analysis—
this is called mindfulness of the Buddha.
When you recollect the Buddha, do not grasp at limited conceptions, do not give rise to frivolous conceptual proliferation,
and do not engage in discrimination. Why is this?
These dharmas are all empty and devoid of intrinsic nature;
they cannot be conceived as having a single characteristic,
namely, that they are nameless.
This is called the true recollection of the Buddha. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata is not designated as form.
It is not called perception;
it is not called mindfulness;
it is not called discrimination.
Neither contrary nor compliant, neither grasping nor rejecting;
it is neither concentration nor wisdom.
Such a person has not yet attained even this with respect to the Buddha.
How much more so regarding mindfulness? Śāriputra,
one who teaches in this way is called a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
If a person accomplishes such characteristics,
they are rare in the world,
for they have attained the non-erroneous, true vision.
This is right view.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
as for right view:
It is called right action, right conduct, the right path, and right understanding.
Being free from inversion, one sees things as they truly are;
therefore, the Tathāgata calls it right view.
If one gives rise to the notion of a self, the notion of a person, or the notion of a sentient being,
it should be known that such a person is practicing erroneously.
The *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* states: "O Śāriputra, regarding evil associates:
there are people who, with pure faith and the other faculties, leave the household life to study the Way."
One encounters evil associates.
As for these evil associates,
they are constantly fond of frivolous play, fickle and flighty, and devoid of shame.
Their speech is distracted and their faculties are unrestrained;
their minds are not one-pointed, being as deluded as white rams.
Those who associate with such evil associates [will suffer].
One loses the fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat;
one even loses the joy of rebirth in heaven,
let alone the path to nirvāṇa.
Śāriputra, such a person follows evil associates;
if born among humans, they will experience separation from their parents, death, and loss.
Relatives will suffer decline and distress, and the land will be destroyed.
One will be born among the eight difficult conditions, abandoning places of happiness,
and encounter evil associates in lands where no Buddha dwells.
If one encounters the era of a Buddha, yet finds no joy in seeing him,
takes no delight in hearing the Dharma,
and does not harmonize with the assembly of the Buddha's disciples.

Regarding the general dhāraṇī for the protection of the dharma common to all sections of the Tripiṭaka, as transmitted by Vajrabodhi to his consecrated disciples: whenever one intends to perform recitation, one must first protect the body, establish the boundary (sīmābandha), and clarify the visualization.
Contemplate the noble deity,
arouse a heart of compassion and pity for sentient beings,
and generate the great vow to dedicate [merit] toward enlightenment.
Only then may one perform the recitation.
One performs four types of recitation using four kinds of rosaries.
The first is vocal recitation (*ghoṣoccāra-japa*).
Second is vajra recitation,
which consists of moving the tongue while keeping the lips closed.
Third is samādhi recitation.
The first is mindfulness through mental recitation; the second is mindfulness through verbal recitation; the third is mindfulness through the meaning of the words;
and the fourth is true recitation, which is the practice according to the literal meaning of the syllables.
This heart-mantra enables the practitioner to swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi and become endowed with all-knowledge.
This is the ultimate truth of all Buddhas,
flowing forth from the wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness);
it is not a manifested product of conditioned phenomena.
Just as a skillfully crafted wish-fulfilling gem can satisfy all desires,
so do all the Buddhas speak with one voice when one contemplates this.
It is solely this luminous clarity, wherein neither body nor mind is perceived;
how much less so any single thing, for there is no phenomenon that is not empty.
If one can cultivate this for a long time until it is matured, it shall become self-realized wisdom.
When performing this visualization,
recite the secret mantra.
One who contemplates this vidyā-mantra [should do so].
One is then able to realize and enter the stage of all consecration maṇḍalas;
regarding the secret dharma-gates of all bodhisattvas, one acts with unhindered freedom as desired.
When performing this contemplation, there is no further prolonging or hastening.
The essential aim lies in realization.
If one can bring each [practice] into correspondence with the mind, then great accomplishment will ensue.
At all times and in all places, one’s mental attention will spontaneously correspond [to the practice].
There is no obstruction whatsoever.
All delusive thoughts, such as greed, hatred, and ignorance, do not need to be deliberately eliminated;
they naturally do not arise, for their nature is eternally pure.
This true dharma-gate is the intrinsically pure mind of all sentient beings, which is called the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
It extends upward from all Buddhas and downward to all sentient beings.
All are entirely equal, without increase or decrease;
it is only because they are shrouded by ignorance and false conceptualization that the essence of these phenomena is unable to manifest.
One who practices this contemplation realizes the samādhi of liberation and omniscience;
this is called the stage of the three types of noble persons prior to the [first] bhūmi.
All their actions then proceed spontaneously in accord with reality.
One naturally enters the first stage (bhūmi) and gives rise to great joy.
The reason for this is that one takes the contemplation of the moon as the skillful means.
It possesses three meanings:
first, the meaning of the purity of the moon,
because it is free from the defilement of sensual desire.
Second is the meaning of the source of purity,
because it is free from the feverish affliction of greed and hatred.
Third is the meaning of luminosity.
Because it is free from delusion,
one should take the moon as a metaphor, yet not form the conceptual understanding that it is the actual moon.
That which belongs to the world is composed of the four great elements and is ultimately subject to destruction.
Because the intrinsically pure mind of sentient beings is without arising or ceasing,
this is the realm of internal realization for all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and is not a sphere of knowledge accessible to the Śrāvakas of the Two Vehicles or to non-Buddhists.
For one who practices this contemplation,
all Buddha-dharmas and the merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are realized through awakening that does not depend on another;
this single dharma encompasses the immeasurable.
In a single instant, they awaken to and enter into all phenomena with sovereign mastery and unimpededness,
gradually ascending from stage to stage.
Those who study this contemplation must not take mere maintenance of mindfulness as the ultimate goal;
they must instead cultivate skillful means through right mindfulness.
Thereafter, one realizes and enters the ultimately pure ocean of Dharma.
The Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom: All Buddhas of the three periods of time, by relying on the Perfection of Wisdom, have attained Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is a great divine mantra;
it is a great illuminating mantra.
This is the unsurpassed mantra;
this is the unequaled mantra.
It can eliminate all suffering; it is true and not false.
The Vajrasamādhi Sūtra, Chapter Six: On the Emptiness of True Nature. Śāriputra said:
"As the World-Honored One has taught, prior to engaging with phenomena, one grasps the fundamental benefit;
this mindfulness is quiescent extinction."
Quiescent extinction is suchness.
It encompasses all virtues and pervades all phenomena;
it is perfectly interfused, non-dual, and inconceivable.
You should know that this Dharma is precisely the Mahāprajñāpāramitā;
it is a great divine mantra.
This is the great vidyā-mantra;
this is the unsurpassed mantra;
this is the unequaled mantra.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is.
Suchness is emptiness."
The fire of the wisdom of the emptiness of intrinsic nature incinerates all fetters;
it is perfectly equal, having equally awakened to the three stages.
The wondrous enlightenment of the three bodies is brilliantly clear and pure within the nine consciousnesses,
devoid of all shadows. If there are sentient beings who possess no other distracting thoughts, [they shall realize it].
At that time, the Bodhisattva constantly manifests transformation bodies to skillfully protect such persons, never departing from their side.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, "Chapter on Māra," states: "If there are sentient beings who practice the *prajñāpāramitā*..."
It is associated with non-recollection and non-attention.
All the kinsmen of Māra become entirely sorrowful and unhappy.
The *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* says: "Śāriputra..."
In my Dharma there are no difficulties;
food, drink, bedding, and medicine are never lacking.
You should simply apply yourselves diligently to the path of the Buddha.
Do not value the worldly offerings of wealth and profit.
Śāriputra, listen well now.
I shall tell you this:
if there is a bhikṣu who practices the path with a single-minded focus,
a thousand billion celestial beings will all with one mind desire to collectively make offerings to him with every kind of delightful requisite.
Śāriputra, when people make offerings to bhikṣus who are practicing seated meditation,
they do not equal those made to devas.
All provisional forms of the Buddha are such [illusory manifestations].
As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Whatever has marks is entirely false and deceptive.
If one perceives me by means of form, or seeks me through sound..."
Such people walk upon a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata.
The *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* says:
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"In other sūtras I have said that if a person sees the Dharma, they see me."
The Tathāgata is neither dharma nor non-dharma; he does not conform to the existence of marks, nor does he rely on the absence of marks—this is the seeing of dharmas.
To see dharmas is to see the original nature. Why is this so?
Devadatta, the foolish people, and all the non-Buddhists all perceive the Buddha by means of his physical body, Śāriputra.
The Tathāgata should not be seen by means of his physical body,
nor should he be seen by means of his voice, Śāriputra.
If a person perceives the Buddha by means of the physical body,
they are far removed from the Buddha. Why is this so?
The Buddha is not called "seeing"; what is called "seeing the Buddha" does not rely on the view of existence or non-existence, which is precisely not relying on right view.

The Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: "One who seeks the Dharma does not cling to seeking the Buddha, does not cling to seeking the Dharma, and does not cling to seeking the Saṃgha; the name 'Dharma' signifies being unstained."
If one is stained by dharmas, even up to nirvāṇa,
this is attachment and not the seeking of the Dharma.
The Dharma is called the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
If one practices the conditioned,
this is seeking the conditioned;
it is not seeking the Dharma.
The Dharma is free from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
If one acts within seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, that is merely seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; it is not the seeking of the Dharma.
Śāriputra, those who seek the Dharma should have no seeking at all regarding any phenomena.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "The unsurpassed treasury of jewels is obtained spontaneously without seeking. If a person does not seek various worldly dharmas, nor do they seek the Buddha-dharma, this is the true seeker of the Dharma.
One who is a true Buddha is a person who recognizes the mind, perceives the nature, and awakens to the principle; such a person is a true Buddha.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "To be free from all marks is precisely what is called 'all Buddhas. Because they are free from existence and free from non-existence;
because they are neither defiled nor pure;
because they are without arising and without essence."
The Prostration of the Dharma Body.
The *Buddhagocaraprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "The Buddha constantly dwells in the world, yet is not defiled by worldly dharmas."
Because you do not discriminate regarding the world,
I pay homage to you who have nothing upon which to rely;
you are like space, without center or periphery.
The bodies of all Buddhas are likewise so,
for their minds are identical to space;
I pay homage to that which is without an object of observation.
I prostrate with universal equanimity;
there is neither prostration nor non-prostration.
With a single prostration, I reach all sentient beings.
To return to the same ultimate reality—that which embodies the essence of suchness—is to neither conform to the existence of substantial characteristics nor rely upon the absence of characteristics.
As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: At that time, Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
I pray that you will explain for me the essential nature of all Buddhas.
The Buddha said:
O Great Wisdom!
Realizing the two kinds of selflessness,
one eliminates the two types of hindrances.
Being free from the two kinds of death and having severed the two kinds of afflictions—
this is the essential nature of the Buddha.
"O Greatly Benevolent One, when Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have realized this Dharma, they too are called Buddhas.
It is for this reason that I teach only the One Vehicle.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
Skillfully knowing the two kinds of selflessness,
one eliminates the two obscurations, the two afflictions,
and inconceivable death.
For this reason, he is called the Tathāgata.
Regarding the provisional Three Jewels: the physical image of the Buddha is the Buddha Jewel;
all sūtras and śāstras, as well as the teachings, are the Dharma Jewel.

Shaving the head, donning the *kāṣāya*, and receiving the two hundred and fifty precepts constitute the Sangha Jewel; yet if one does not recognize the mind and does not see its nature, there is no jewel at all.
For those who have seen their nature, the true Three Jewels are fully present.
The Vimalakīrti Sūtra states:
The Bodhisattva Śāntendriya said, "The Buddha,
the Dharma, and the Saṅgha constitute a duality."
The Buddha is the Dharma;
the Dharma is the Sangha.
These are the Three Jewels.
All are unconditioned characteristics,
equal to empty space;
all dharmas are likewise.

One who is able to practice in accordance with this enters the gate of non-dual dharmas; by not following the practice of existence and not relying on the practice of non-existence, such a person is one who has departed from all dharmas.
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* says: "If one realizes this dharma through bodily realization..."
Nor does one perceive phenomena apart from the body, nor the body apart from phenomena;
within this contemplation, one perceives no duality.
One does not perceive the mark of non-duality;
thus, even while knowing and seeing what is present before one, one does not perceive it—
this is called the noble silence.
If there are bodhisattvas who,
regarding phenomena that are superior, middling,
or inferior, neither grasp nor reject them.
This is called practicing for enlightenment:
not discriminating between what is dharma and what is non-dharma as being two.
Nor can they not be non-dual;
this is called practicing bodhi.
If they were dual, they would be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
That which is neither of these two is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
To remain free from these two extremes is called practicing bodhi.
Such a person has transcended the stage of ordinary beings,
yet has not yet entered the fixed position of the Dharma;
they are noble even before attaining the fruit.
This is the field of merit for the world.
When practicing the Buddha-way,
there is no dharma to be abandoned or forsaken.
Furthermore, there is no dharma to be received;
this is called the characteristic of bodhi.
It is entirely free from all conceptualization.
This is precisely the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked Siyi Bodhisattva:
"What is meant by 'cultivating the path'?"
The Bodhisattva Siyi replied,
"If one does not discriminate between what is dharma and what is non-dharma, remaining free from these two marks,
this is called the cultivation of the path."
He asked again,
"What is called the cultivation of the path?
He replied:
One does not fall into existence, nor does one fall into non-existence, nor does one discriminate between existence and non-existence.
To practice in this manner is called the cultivation of the path.
He asked again:
Why is it not seen?
Answer:
It is said that because one is free from the two marks, it is not seen.
Not seeing is precisely seeing.
If one’s preaching of the Dharma does not contradict the Buddha, does not contradict the Dharma, and does not contradict the Sangha, it is called the preaching of the Dharma.

To know that the Dharma is itself the Buddha is the Buddha Jewel; to be free from marks is the Dharma, which is the Dharma Jewel; and to be unconditioned is the Sangha, which is the Sangha Jewel. When a single person realizes their nature, [all three Jewels are realized].
It is clear that the Three Jewels are fully present. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"To see one's nature and attain the Buddha-way—apart from seeing one's nature, there is no other dharma-gate by which one can transcend the three realms and attain Buddhahood; such a thing is impossible. The provisional precepts are established as a cause for the transgression of prohibitive precepts. This is the regulation of the precepts.
This precept is a precept of expedient means;
it is an incomplete teaching.
It permits one to study for five years, and if one does not relinquish [the practice] after five years, one is truly a non-Buddhist (tīrthika).
Regarding this person who is fully possessed of wrong views, the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* states:
The Buddha told Śāriputra, "I speak of the teacher, not of the recipient.
Śāriputra, [this is so].
Within my Dharma, there are many such teachings of overweening pride.
Śāriputra, if those who receive these teachings have been ordained for five years, they will not be able to abandon them all.
If one does not personally attain realization through diligent application and energetic effort within these teachings as thus instructed,
and if there is no bhikṣu to whom they go for consultation,
I declare that such a person, even if they have been ordained for five years, is still called one of wrong view.
They mingle with the teachings of non-Buddhists and follow the instructions of Māra. Śāriputra,
if there is a bhikṣu who, having received such teachings, hears the Dharma of emptiness and non-apprehension.
He immediately realized for himself:
"All that I previously accepted was false view;
regarding these dharmas of emptiness where nothing is apprehended, I have no regret."
Having deeply penetrated and thoroughly understood [reality], they do not rely on any view of a self or a person. Śāriputra,
I declare that such a person is called one who practices the pure holy life (brahmacarya).
The *Dharmapada* says: "If one speaks of those who uphold the precepts,
yet lack goodness and proper deportment,
their nature of morality is like empty space."
Those who uphold it are deluded and inverted.
The *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* states:

"For those who preach the precepts, because of unwholesome pride and like the waves of the ocean, when the ocean of the eight consciousnesses in the ground of the mind is clarified and the flow of the ninth consciousness is purified, the wind does not move and the waves do not arise; the nature of the precepts is equal to emptiness, yet those who uphold it are deluded and inverted."
The *Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśa-sūtra* says: "If a person discriminates precepts, there are no precepts;
if one has a view regarding precepts,"
This is indeed the loss of precepts;
that precepts and non-precepts are of one and the same mark—
knowing this is to be a teacher of the Way.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "There are two kinds of precepts.
The first is that which one naturally maintains by one's own nature;
the second is that which requires the instruction and admonition of others."
If one encounters a preceptor and undergoes the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*,
only then does one obtain the precepts.
Even after having obtained the precepts, one must rely upon the instructions and exhortations of the upādhyāya, various teachers, fellow students, and virtuous friends.
Thus one knows that whether advancing or halting,
listening to or preaching the Dharma, and maintaining all formal dignities,
these are called "relying on the instructions of others."
The *Brahmacarya-parivarta* of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "If precepts constitute the holy life (*brahmacarya*), is the ritual ground (*maṇḍala*) the precepts?
Thus it is asked.
Is purity itself the precept?
Is the instruction in dignified deportment the precept?
Is the threefold proclamation of the *karmavācanā* the precept?
Is the Upādhyāya the precept?
Is the Ācārya the precept?
Is shaving the hair the precept?
Is wearing the kashaya robe the precept?
Is begging for food the precept?
Is right livelihood the precept?
Having observed in this way, one has nothing to grasp regarding the body,
nothing to cling to regarding cultivation,
and nothing to dwell upon regarding phenomena.
The past has already ceased;
the future has not yet arrived;
the present is empty and quiescent.
There is no agent of action;
there is no experiencer of retribution.
This world does not move.
That world does not change.
Among these, what dharma is called the holy life (*brahmacarya*),
and from where does it come?
To whom does this body belong? By whom was it made?
Is it conditioned or is it unconditioned?
True precepts mean that all sentient beings inherently possess buddha-nature from the very beginning.
Those who uphold true precepts are people who recognize the mind and perceive its nature.
At the moment of perceiving this nature, conceptual thoughts do not arise.
Without giving rise to conceptual discrimination or the habitual tendencies of outflows,

one enters into that which is beyond precepts— neither self nor other, neither defiled nor pure, without self, without person, without thought, without discrimination, without master, without ruler, without stinginess, without attachment, and requiring nothing at all.
All desires are eternally stilled, equal to empty space;
like insentient matter, body and mind have no self-agency.
Transgression and observance of precepts are non-dual.
One who knows thus is a true upholder of the precepts.
Regarding the preaching of impure Dharma, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "In future ages, there shall be..."
Clad in the saṃghāṭī robe,
they falsely propound existence and non-existence,
thereby destroying my True Dharma.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Those deluded people speak of the existence of three vehicles;
they do not say that there is only mind and no external objects."
All deluded non-Buddhists falsely perceive the agent and the acted-upon;
they are all attached to the views of existence and non-existence.
Therefore, there is no liberation;
nirvana is apart from mind and consciousness.
This one dharma alone is real.
The storehouse consciousness is called "mind" (citta);
the faculty of reflection is taken as "intellect" (manas).
The mind is like a white garment.
The habitual tendencies of consciousness constitute defilement;
being stained by these habitual tendencies of defilement,
the mindful mind does not manifest.
If one were to establish all phenomena by grasping at their literal meaning,
then because of that establishment, [it would follow that]...
Upon death, they fall into hell.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Those people are foolish and do not understand."
Verbal expression arises and ceases,
but the meaning neither arises nor ceases.
All verbal expressions fall within the realm of letters.
In terms of meaning, it does not fall [into extremes],
because it is free from existence and free from non-existence,
and because it is without arising and without essence.
The Pure Dharma Discourse (*Śuddhadharmadeśanā-sūtra*) states in the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra*: "Śāriputra,
this person is furthermore able to maintain the precepts with purity."
It is without flaw;
neither defiled nor pure;
praised by those with sovereign wisdom, it is capable of being fully possessed within oneself.
When one practices in accordance with meditative concentration and delights in sitting in meditation,
such a bhikṣu, Śāriputra, I also permit to receive offerings.
Having personally realized the Dharma-body, they are free from doubt or regret.
I permit such a person to sit on a high seat and preach the Dharma;
even if one sees an ordinary person who purely maintains the precepts, [they may do so].
The mind does not cling to the doctrines of non-Buddhist scriptures;
with single-minded diligence, one seeks the supreme fruits of the śramaṇa.
One does not crave gain and honor, but skillfully and definitively explains the teachings.
His extensive learning and vast analogies are like the great ocean;
even at the cost of his life, he never speaks falsely.
He takes no pleasure in litigation, benefiting both himself and others.
I speak only of the pure, supreme ultimate truth;
that which is taught is thus, Śāriputra.
I listen to the Dharma being taught in this manner:
that which the Tathāgata has spoken ensures that all phenomena do not contradict one another;
he teaches it as the exposition of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Śāriputra, there are monks who seek profit;
though they have left the household life for the sake of the Buddha, they violate the precepts.
Of what use is preaching the Dharma?
Why is this so, Śāriputra?
In my sūtras I have said:
if a person cannot bring themselves to tranquility and cannot protect themselves,
they may yet enable others to attain tranquility and protect themselves.
This is impossible.
